aliases: Camellia sinensis var. assamica cv. Menghai-dayecha
processing: A cultivar rather than a finished tea: its leaf can be made into black tea, green tea or pu-erh. As raw pu-erh it would follow the usual path for the class: withered, pan-fired, rolled, sun-dried and often pressed.
harvest_season: An early variety: spring picking starts in early March, and the one-bud-three-leaf flush peaks in mid-March.
appearance_dry: As with other large-leaf Yunnan material made into raw pu-erh, expect long, dark olive-green leaves with some pale downy buds.
appearance_liquor: As a young raw pu-erh, typically clear golden yellow.
appearance_wet: Large elongated or elliptical leaves, which is the variety's defining trait, opening olive-green.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about the taste of the cultivar on its own. Raw pu-erh from Yunnan large-leaf varieties is typically full and bitter up front, with a returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Advice for raw pu-erh from this leaf. Large-leaf tea turns bitter quickly, so keep the first steeps short. Black or green tea from the same cultivar needs its own class's method.

vintage_note: The cultivar is not sold under one vintage rule, because the same leaf goes into different teas. Green tea from it is usual as the current year's spring picking, black tea as a recent harvest, and raw pu-erh by harvest year, young or aged. It is seldom named on a label, so ask the seller what the leaf is.
description:
Menghai Dayecha is a tea plant before it is a tea: a tree-form, large-leaf, early-budding variety from Nannuo Mountain in Menghai County, Yunnan. You will rarely see it on a label, but it is useful to know as a piece of the Yunnan large-leaf picture.

The plant grows tall with a clear main trunk and big long-elliptical leaves. It is grown mainly in southern Yunnan, and on a large scale in Sichuan, Guangxi, Guizhou and Guangdong too, so a tea from this cultivar need not come from Menghai at all.

Its leaf suits black tea, green tea and pu-erh. We file it with raw pu-erh because that is its home context, but the cup depends on the processing. Little is recorded about how it tastes as a single cultivar; large-leaf raw pu-erh in general is bitter and full early on, with sweetness coming back afterwards.

When buying, treat the name as information about the plant and nothing more. It tells you neither where the leaf grew nor how old the trees are, so those are the questions to ask.
history: The variety originated on Nannuo Mountain in Menghai County, and it also goes by the older names Nanman tea and Fohai tea. In 1985 China's national crop variety committee recognised it as a national variety, under the number GS13014-1985.
